faq.q: Where does meteor shower dust come from?
faq.a: Mostly from comets. As a comet nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas and releases dust, which spreads along its orbit. The Perseids come from Comet Swift-Tuttle, and the Geminids from an asteroid called Phaethon.

faq.q: Why do meteor showers happen on the same dates every year?
faq.a: Earth passes the same point in its orbit on about the same date every year. If a comet's dust trail crosses our orbit there, we meet that dust again each year at the same time.
asks: Why are the Perseids in August every year?

faq.a: The radiant is the point in the sky that a shower's meteors seem to come from. The grains all travel in parallel, so, like railway lines meeting in the distance, their paths seem to spread out from one spot.
asks: Why do shower meteors come from one point?

faq.q: When are the best meteor showers?
faq.a: Two of the best are the Perseids, peaking around 12 August, and the Geminids, peaking around 13 to 14 December. On a dark, moonless night each can show around 100 meteors an hour.
asks: When can I see a meteor shower?

faq.q: How do I watch a meteor shower?
faq.a: Find a dark place away from city lights, lie back, and look at a wide area of sky. Give your eyes 20 minutes to adjust; no telescope is needed. The best time is usually after midnight.
asks: Do I need a telescope to see shooting stars?

facts: The Perseid meteor shower comes from dust left by Comet Swift-Tuttle and peaks around 12 August.
The Geminid shower comes from the asteroid 3200 Phaethon and peaks around 13 to 14 December.
Meteor showers are named after the constellation that contains their radiant.
